newsitem.title: RUSSIA: SOCCER-RUSSIAN LEAGUE DEBATES RIVAL CSKA CLAIMS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-RUSSIAN LEAGUE DEBATES RIVAL CSKA CLAIMS.

text.p: The Russian football league's disciplinary committee met on Tuesday to study two rival claims for CSKA Moscow's place in next season's premier league.

League officials said discussions were likely to run on late into the evening as the two pretenders to the right to represent the Army Central Sporting Club (CSKA) slugged out who had the controlling stake in the army's professional soccer side.

But a spokesman for the Russian Football Union, which oversees all soccer in Russia, said its separate, legal committee had ruled in favour of the squad trained by Alexander Tarkhanov, who led CSKA to fifth in the league last year.
"Its conclusions were in favour of Tarkhanov," spokesman Yuri Yudin told Reuters.
The league, however, must make its own ruling.
A rival team, which has the backing of CSKA's Russian army sponsor, is also in training in Moscow under ex-Zenit St Petersburg coach Pavel Sadyrin. The 1997 season opens in March.

The army, in the shape of Colonel Alexander Baranovsky, who heads all of CSKA's manifold sporting activities, sacked Tarkhanov earlier this month and replaced him with former Russian national coach Sadyrin, who was fired by Zenit in November.
Barkhanov insists the army owns 60 percent of the CSKA Moscow soccer club.

But Tarkhanov has the backing of Moscow businessman Oleg Kim, who also owns shares in the team, and is still coaching what is effectively the bulk of the 1996 squad, including newly transferred Nigerian World Cup defender Augustine Eguavoen.
Tarkhanov told Sport Express newspaper on Tuesday that, contrary to Baranovsky's statements, Kim owned a 68 percent majority of the club, giving him the right to field the team.

"Everything can be settled at the disciplinary committee meeting on January 21," Tarkhanov said. "I'm sure it will be in our favour," he added, saying he expected a full meeting of the league council on Thursday to confirm that decision.

The dispute over soccer is a replay of a monumental falling out at CSKA's ice hockey club. Colonel Baranovsky and the army came off worst in a clash with Viktor Tikhonov, who coached the world-beating Soviet hockey sides of the 1980s.

A series of legal battles has left Tikhonov in charge of the CSKA Moscow team which takes part in the top Russian hockey league and in European competition. A separate CSKA team controlled by Baranovsky competes at a lower level.
